label: AQ 0005
title: The tool that can do anything

questions.q: Can't you just check the code before running it?
questions.a: A scanner helps, but code can reach the same dangerous call in a roundabout way. The limits have to live where it runs.

questions.q: When would you keep plain tool calls?
questions.a: One-call tasks, where starting a sandbox costs more than the round trip it saves; actions that need a person's approval each time; and weaker models that write unreliable code.

teach.title: How it works: what you build before code is safe

questions.q: Why are models better at writing code than calling tools?
questions.a: Cloudflare's explanation: models have seen huge amounts of real code in training and very few tool calls. Code also lets them loop and keep results in variables.

teach.title: How it works: what you build before code is safe

questions.q: Why isn't “code can have bugs” the real reason?
questions.a: Tool calls can carry wrong values too. The real difference is that a tool call is one checked action from a fixed menu, while a program can do anything the language allows.

questions.q: Where do the token savings in the Google Drive to Salesforce example come from?
questions.a: The transcript moves from one tool to the other inside the program, so it never passes through the model's context: 150,000 tokens became 2,000.

teach.title: How it works: what you build before code is safe

questions.q: Name four things a sandbox setup needs before code execution is safe.
questions.a: A sealed place to run (a sandbox), hard limits set from outside, no internet except named destinations, and no keys inside.
